question: For each packet candidate, can a credible learner who lacks that full competence still understand and explain Pythagoras' theorem through another route, or does the candidate supply an unavoidable conceptual foundation? Check for missing core foundations and for converse or coordinate applications that depend on the target rather than precede it.

votes.rationale: A learner may be shown a marked corner, but understanding the theorem's scope requires recognising that the marked angle is right; without that, they cannot identify when the relation applies.
A learner can understand the formula from a labelled right triangle without describing every right-triangle property; the broader description gives useful context but is not required.
Perpendicularity explains why the sides form a right angle, but a learner can use a right-angle marker and explain the theorem without general parallel-line knowledge.
Square areas provide a concrete proof or interpretation, but a learner can explain squared side lengths numerically without knowing rectangle or square area formulas.
To explain a^2+b^2=c^2 rather than recite it, the learner must interpret multiplication and powers in the expression; the full notation skill is the closest available match.
Arithmetic supports worked examples, but a learner can explain the invariant relation with symbolic or simple values and does not need the full four-operation competence first.
Calculator roots help produce decimal answers, while a learner can explain the theorem and leave an answer as a square root or use perfect squares.
Evaluating an unknown from a formula supports applications, but a learner can understand the theorem by explaining the known-side relation without solving a general formula.
Changing the subject helps solve for a missing side, yet rearrangement can be demonstrated with one concrete equation and is not needed to explain the geometric claim.
Triangle area is an explanatory bridge for an area dissection proof, but numerical examples or a direct geometric statement let a learner explain Pythagoras without triangle-area calculation.
Composite-area procedures are one proof or application technique; a learner can explain Pythagoras using a single right triangle and the squared-side relation.
Triangle properties can support interpreting the diagram, but a learner needs only the right-angle configuration and can be taught the theorem without the full properties catalogue.
Rectangle and square area calculations support an area proof, but they are unnecessary for a numerical or symbolic explanation of the theorem.
Using the theorem for an unknown side requires understanding squaring and square roots; a learner unable to relate these inverse operations cannot explain the complete side-finding use.
Substitution connects measured sides to the formula in practice, but a learner can explain the theorem abstractly or with already-labelled values without this general competence.
Rearranging to find a missing side is a useful application bridge, but it is downstream algebra and not necessary to understand what the theorem asserts.
Accurate positive arithmetic makes examples workable, but an explanation can use simple perfect-square values or symbolic quantities without full procedural mastery.
Consistent units prevent invalid comparisons in applied examples, but a learner can explain the dimensionless relationship in one unit or use a diagram with equal units.
Scale-drawing interpretation is an application context; a learner can understand and explain the theorem from a direct labelled diagram without reading a scale.
Recognising a triangle and its sides helps read a diagram, but the target can introduce the one needed shape and does not require classifying all basic 2D shapes.
Triangle angle sums do not explain the squared-length relation and are not needed when the right angle is given; this is a separate geometry result.
Determining whether a triangle is right from its lengths is the converse direction, which uses Pythagoras rather than preparing a learner to understand the forward theorem.
Calculator powers ease computation, but a learner can understand the theorem through mental perfect squares, symbolic notation, or a diagram without calculator skill.
A learner must understand that squaring a length means multiplying it by itself and yields square units to explain what each term represents, rather than memorising symbols.
The theorem equates squared lengths, not lengths themselves; without distinguishing a length from its square and tracking units, a learner cannot give a coherent conceptual explanation.
The hypotenuse determines which side is c and must be identified to state or apply the theorem correctly; a learner who cannot locate it cannot explain the scope of the relation.
The theorem is an equality of quantities under right-triangle conditions. A learner can calculate examples mechanically without this, but cannot explain what the equation claims.
Recovering a side from its square is central to using Pythagoras for unknown lengths; inverse-square reasoning is required for that conceptual use, even if numerical extraction is deferred.
Unit names support interpreting real measurements, but the theorem can be understood with abstract lengths or a single consistent unit; mass and volume units are extraneous.
Square-unit area language strengthens a geometric explanation, but a learner can explain the theorem numerically without measuring areas or converting cm2 and m2.
Viewing a squared length as a square's area supplies a powerful area-dissection bridge, but direct numerical and symbolic routes leave the theorem understandable without it.
Preserving equality during rearrangement supports solving variants, but the un-rearranged theorem can be understood and explained without general equality-preservation reasoning.
Integer arithmetic supports clean examples, but it is narrower than the target's conceptual need and can be replaced by simple positive values or symbolic reasoning.
Decomposing arbitrary figures into 2D shapes is not an explanatory prerequisite; a single right triangle diagram suffices and composite decomposition is a later application route.
Composite-plane-area calculation is an optional area proof or application. A learner can explain the theorem without learning this broad procedure.
Letters make the general relationship visible and support unknown-side notation, but the theorem can first be understood with named or numerical side lengths.
To explain a theorem rather than report a pattern from examples, the learner must understand that the relation is general for all right triangles; otherwise the central claim is missing.
Recognising the right triangle and locating its hypotenuse is the domain condition of the theorem. Without it, a learner cannot say when the relation applies.
The formula's powers must be understood as products of a number by itself; otherwise the learner can only memorise notation and cannot explain the squared-length relationship.
The full classification of acute, obtuse and reflex angles is unnecessary; only recognising a right angle matters, which can be supplied independently of the broader skill.
Cartesian coordinates are an alternative representation and proof route. A learner can explain the theorem geometrically without coordinates, which are often introduced after the target.
Coordinate geometry problems are downstream applications and may themselves use the distance formula derived from Pythagoras; they cannot be required as a prior foundation.
Similar-triangle proofs can justify one derivation, but a learner can understand and explain the theorem from its statement, diagram, or area argument without this later proof skill.
General triangle-proof technique is broader than the target and not needed for conceptual use; requiring it confuses a formal proof route with prerequisite understanding.
Area gives a concrete bridge through squares on the three sides, but it is not unavoidable because numerical, symbolic, or direct geometric explanations remain available.
